opus-5.5.text:
I think there's some truth to it, but it's often overstated. Benchmarks absolutely do get saturated, and faster than they used to. When we released MMLU, models were barely above chance on a lot of the subjects, and within a few years frontier models were in the high eighties and nineties. MATH followed a similar arc. So the half-life of a benchmark has gotten much shorter, and that's a real phenomenon people should take seriously.

But "saturated" isn't the same as "AI can do everything we care about." A few distinctions matter.

First, a lot of the saturated benchmarks were multiple-choice or short-answer knowledge tests. Those measure something real, but they're relatively easy to climb. They say less about whether a model can carry out long-horizon tasks, do original research, or operate reliably as an agent in messy environments. On those fronts, performance is often still quite weak or very inconsistent.

Second, near the ceiling you have to account for label noise. If a dataset has a few percent of questions that are ambiguous or mislabeled, then going from 90 to 93 might just be the model learning the dataset's quirks. That's partly saturation and partly the benchmark running out of signal.

Third, there's contamination. When test questions leak into pretraining data, scores get inflated, so some apparent saturation is memorization rather than capability. That's one reason it's valuable to keep private held-out sets and to keep making new evaluations.

That's the motivation behind efforts like Humanity's Last Exam: go to the frontier of expert knowledge, gather questions that experts can verify but current models can't answer, and filter adversarially against the strongest models. That buys you headroom. Even those will eventually get climbed, and that's fine. A benchmark isn't meant to last forever. It's meant to tell you something during the window when it can discriminate between systems.

So my overall take is that the claim "benchmarks are saturated" is mostly an argument for building harder and more realistic benchmarks. It's not an argument that measurement is pointless. If anything, as capabilities get more economically and strategically important, we need better measurement, especially of things like autonomous task completion, dangerous capabilities, and real-world economic value, not just exam-style questions. The worst outcome would be for people to give up on evaluation right when the stakes are highest.

r001.rationale: The response says performance remains weak or inconsistent on long-horizon tasks, original research, and agent work in messy environments.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks can be climbed within a few years, but does not suggest creating benchmarks that take roughly one to two years to solve.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the claim is half right and the half that's right is the uninteresting half.

Yes, a lot of benchmarks saturate fast. MMLU went from "frontier models get 40%" to "everything's at 88-90%" in about three years. GSM8K is done. HumanEval is done. If you look at the set of benchmarks people were citing in 2021, almost all of them are effectively solved. So in that narrow sense, sure.

But I'd push back on the framing in a couple of ways.

First, saturation is partly a design choice. When we built MMLU, the goal was to make something that was hard for the models of 2020 but tractable enough that you could measure progress on it. That's a different goal from making something that stays hard for ten years. If you're measuring capabilities during a period of rapid progress, you should expect your instruments to get used up. A thermometer that only goes to 40 degrees isn't broken, it's just the wrong tool once the temperature goes past that. That's why we built Humanity's Last Exam, to deliberately ask: what's the hardest closed-ended academic question set we can assemble, where experts are confident the answers are correct and the models currently can't do them? And even there, I don't expect it to last forever. I'd be surprised if it lasted more than a few years. That's fine. It tells you something while it lasts.

Second, and this is the more important point, "saturated" is often conflated with "the model actually has the capability." Those aren't the same thing. There's a real issue with contamination, with models being trained on paraphrases of test questions, and with the gap between doing well on a fixed question set and doing the underlying task robustly. A model can get 90% on a math benchmark and still fall over when you rephrase the problem slightly or introduce a distractor. So when someone says "benchmarks are saturated, therefore the models are superhuman at X," I'd want to see the cross-check. Saturation is evidence, but it's weak evidence on its own.

Third, there are whole categories that are clearly not saturated, and they tend to be the ones that matter most. Long-horizon agentic tasks, where you have to do something over hours or days with lots of steps and tool use, models still fail at those in ways that aren't captured by short question-answer formats. Anything requiring genuine novelty, like producing a research result that's actually new rather than retrieving and recombining. And then there's the safety-relevant stuff: honesty under pressure, whether the model will sandbag, whether it behaves consistently when it thinks it's not being watched. Those are hard to benchmark precisely because the thing you're measuring is adversarial to being measured.

So my overall take is: the easy stuff got easy, as it should. That's not a crisis for evaluation, it's a signal that evaluation needs to move up the ladder. What would actually worry me is if we stopped being able to construct any task that the models fail at. We're not there. And the moment we are, we'd better have other ways of knowing what these systems are doing than exam scores.

r001.rationale: The response identifies several unsaturated dimensions—long-horizon agentic tasks, genuine novelty, and safety-relevant behavior—and says models still fail at these tasks.

r002.rationale: It says Humanity’s Last Exam might not remain difficult for more than a few years, but does not suggest a one-to-two-year solve time.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s too broad a claim. Some benchmarks saturate quickly, but that doesn’t mean we’ve run out of things to measure. It can mean that the benchmark was too easy, that it covered a narrow capability, or that people optimized heavily for it. Those are different explanations, and we should distinguish them.

There’s also a difference between getting a high score and solving the underlying problem. A model can do very well on a fixed set of questions and still be unreliable when you change the formulation or put it in a different setting. So you want to look at generalization, robustness, and the kinds of mistakes it still makes, rather than just the headline number.

I wouldn’t conclude that benchmarks are useless. I’d conclude that we need harder measurements and a broader collection of them. A benchmark is a particular instrument for measuring progress; it isn’t a complete definition of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unreliability under changed formulations and remaining mistakes, but does not state that models perform poorly across many evaluation dimensions.

r002.rationale: The response calls for harder measurements and broader benchmarks, but gives no estimate that a benchmark could take one to two years to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s overstated. Some benchmarks saturate quickly, but there’s a selection effect: people pay attention to the benchmarks where systems are making rapid progress, and then generalize from those to all benchmarks. There are still plenty of tasks where models perform poorly.

You also have to distinguish getting a high score from solving the underlying problem. A model might do well on a particular distribution of questions while remaining brittle under small changes, or while requiring much more assistance than a human would. That doesn’t make the benchmark useless, but it limits what you can conclude from it.

So I’d assess these claims benchmark by benchmark. What capability does it measure? Is there still room to distinguish systems? And does improvement on it translate into something we actually care about? Saturation is a reason to develop harder or more informative evaluations, not a reason to give up on measurement.

r001.rationale: The response says there are still plenty of tasks where models perform poorly.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest a benchmark solving timeframe of roughly one to two years.
